question: How did Chinese sources describe the Roman empire?
answer: Chinese sources described Rome (Da Qin) as a distant western kingdom located "west of Anxi (Parthia) and Tiaozhi... and west of the Great Sea," reached by a long sea voyage that could take from two months to three years depending on the wind [S1]. The Weilüe describes its geography in detail, noting it had "more than four hundred smaller cities and towns," extended "several thousand li in all directions," and that its king's capital lay near a river mouth with outer walls "made of stone" [S1]. The Hou Hanshu records a specific historical contact: in 166 CE, during the reign of Emperor Huan, "the king of Da Qin... Andun... sent envoys from beyond the frontiers through Rinan... to offer elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn, and turtle shell," which the text calls the first direct communication between the two countries [S3]. However, the same source expresses doubt about this embassy, stating that "the tribute brought was neither precious nor rare, raising suspicion that the accounts [of the 'envoys'] might be exaggerated" [S3]. A separate archaeological source notes that "Chinese historical texts claim the Romans first landed" in the vicinity of Óc Eo before proceeding further into China for this 166 CE diplomatic contact, though the text of that claim itself is not given [S2].

english.text: The kingdom of Da Qin (Rome) is also called Lijian. It is west of Anxi (Parthia) and Tiaozhi (Characene and Susiana), and west of the Great Sea. From the city of Angu (Gerrha), on the frontier of Anxi (Parthia), you take a boat and cut directly across to Haixi ('West of the Sea' = Egypt). With favourable winds it takes two months; if the winds are slow, perhaps a year; if there is no wind, perhaps three years... This country (the Roman Empire) has more than four hundred smaller cities and towns. It extends several thousand li in all directions. The king has his capital (that is, the city of Rome) close to the mouth of a river (the Tiber). The outer walls of the city are made of stone.
english.attribution: John E. Hill, 'The Peoples of the West from the Weilüe by Yu Huan: A Third Century Chinese Account Composed between 239 and 265 CE', draft annotated translation, University of Washington Silk Road Seattle project.

english.text: The remains found at Oc Eo include pottery, tools, jewelry, casts for making jewelry, coins, and religious statues. Among the finds are gold jewellery imitating coins from the Roman Empire of the Antonine period... Oc Eo was near Chinese-controlled Jiaozhou and the region where Chinese historical texts claim the Romans first landed before venturing further into China to conduct diplomacy in 166.

In the ninth yanxi year [166 CE], during the reign of Emperor Huan, the king of Da Qin (the Roman Empire), Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus), sent envoys from beyond the frontiers through Rinan (Commandery on the central Vietnamese coast), to offer elephant tusks, rhinoceros horn, and turtle shell. This was the very first time there was [direct] communication [between the two countries]. The tribute brought was neither precious nor rare, raising suspicion that the accounts [of the 'envoys'] might be exaggerated.
english.attribution: John E. Hill, '"Chapter on the Western Regions" from Hou Hanshu 88', draft annotated translation, University of Washington Silk Road Seattle project.

english.text: 경주 98호 남분 유리병 및 잔 (慶州 九十八號 南墳 琉璃甁 및 盞) — Glass Ewer and Cups from the South Mound of Tomb No. 98, Gyeongju. Designated National Treasure No. 193, 7 December 1978.
Signature on the silver cups: [ΧEIPI]ΣΟΦΟΣ ЄΠΟΙΕΙ ('Cheirisophos made [this]'); engraved owner's name: SILIVS.

Contents include gold, silver, spear shafts, shield boards, ropes, cords, leather, textiles, tools, wooden vessels, spoons, beads, four horses and a cow. The deposit contains 194 Roman denarii, four barbarous imitations, and a sestertius.
